name: JavaScript
description: Coercion, closures, the event loop, prototypes and the modern language features that replaced the old workarounds.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What JavaScript is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is JavaScript, and where does it run?
cards.answer: The programming language of the web: every browser runs it to make pages interactive. It also runs outside the browser on servers and tools via runtimes such as Node.js, Deno and Bun.
cards.explanation: HTML describes a page's content, CSS its appearance, and JavaScript its behaviour — responding to clicks, fetching data, updating the page. Node.js (2009) took the same language to the server, which is why one language can now cover front end, back end and build tooling.

cards.prompt: Where did JavaScript come from, and what is ECMAScript?
cards.answer: Brendan Eich created it at Netscape in 1995, famously in about ten days. ECMAScript is the official standard for the language, maintained by Ecma's TC39 committee; JavaScript is the name everyone uses for implementations of it.
cards.explanation: Despite the name, JavaScript is unrelated to Java — the name was a marketing decision. New features arrive in yearly ECMAScript editions (ES2015 brought `let`, `const`, classes, arrow functions and modules; later editions added async/await and more).

cards.prompt: How is JavaScript executed?
cards.answer: By a JavaScript engine — V8 (Chrome, Node.js), SpiderMonkey (Firefox) or JavaScriptCore (Safari). The engine parses the source and uses just-in-time (JIT) compilation to turn hot code into fast machine code while it runs.
cards.explanation: You never compile JavaScript yourself: you ship source text and the engine handles the rest. JavaScript is single-threaded per page or process; it stays responsive by handling events and asynchronous work through an event loop rather than by blocking.

cards.prompt: What does a minimal JavaScript program look like?
cards.answer: One statement that logs to the console. In a browser it appears in the developer tools console; under Node.js (`node hello.js`) it prints to the terminal.
cards.explanation: `console.log` is the universal "print". Statements are usually ended with semicolons (optional in most cases, thanks to automatic semicolon insertion), and blocks use braces `{ }` rather than indentation.

cards.prompt: What kind of language is JavaScript: typing, memory and paradigms?
cards.answer: Dynamically and weakly typed: variables have no fixed type and values are converted implicitly (`"5" * 2` is `10`). Memory is garbage collected. It mixes functional style (first-class functions, closures) with prototype-based objects; `class` syntax sits on top of prototypes.
cards.explanation: Weak typing is the source of the famous quirks (`[] + {}`, `==` coercions), which is why style guides insist on `===`. TypeScript exists largely to add static types on top of JavaScript for bigger codebases.

resources.title: MDN — JavaScript data types and data structures

cards.prompt: What are npm and `package.json`?
cards.answer: npm is JavaScript's package registry and the command-line tool that installs from it. `package.json` describes a project: its name, scripts (`npm run build`) and dependencies. A lock file (`package-lock.json`) pins the exact versions installed.
cards.explanation: The npm registry is the largest package registry in the world. Alternatives such as pnpm, Yarn and Bun use the same registry and `package.json` format. Installed packages land in a project-local `node_modules` folder, never globally by default.

modules.name: Semantics & Coercion
modules.description: Types, equality, scoping and the behaviours JavaScript is famous for.

cards.answer: `==` coerces operands to a common type before comparing; `===` compares type and value with no coercion.

left.title: == (loose)
points: `null == undefined` is true (the one useful case)
Non-transitive in places — hard to reason about

right.title: === (strict)
points: The default choice in every style guide

cards.explanation: Use `===` everywhere except the idiom `x == null`, which tests for null or undefined in one go. For NaN use `Number.isNaN`; for the SameValue semantics that distinguish -0 use `Object.is`.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.answer:
undefined
ReferenceError
cards.explanation: `var` declarations are hoisted and initialised to `undefined`. `let`/`const` are hoisted too, but sit in the temporal dead zone until the declaration executes — touching them first throws a ReferenceError. That is a feature: it turns a silent bug into a loud one.

cards.prompt: What determines the value of `this` in a JavaScript function?
cards.answer: The call site, in this precedence: `new` binding → explicit `call`/`apply`/`bind` → method call (the object before the dot) → default (undefined in strict mode, globalThis otherwise). Arrow functions ignore all of it and inherit `this` lexically.
cards.explanation: `this` is not the defining scope — it is decided when the function is invoked. `const f = obj.method; f()` loses the receiver. Arrow functions have no `this` of their own, which is exactly why they are the right choice for callbacks inside methods.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.explanation: `var` is function-scoped, so all three closures share one binding that ends at 3. `let` creates a fresh binding per iteration — the loop head is re-bound each pass — so each closure captures its own value.

cards.prompt: How does property lookup work on a JavaScript object?
cards.answer: The engine checks the object's own properties, then walks `[[Prototype]]` (`Object.getPrototypeOf`) link by link until it finds the key or reaches null.
cards.explanation: `class` is syntax over this: methods live on `Ctor.prototype`, and every instance links to it. This is why adding a method to a prototype affects existing instances, and why shadowing a prototype property with an own property hides it rather than overwriting it.

resources.title: MDN — Inheritance and the prototype chain

cards.prompt: Why does mutating the copy still change the original?
cards.answer: Spread is a **shallow** copy — `copy.tags` is the same array reference. Deep-clone with `structuredClone(original)` or copy nested values explicitly.
cards.explanation: `{...o}` and `Object.assign({}, o)` copy one level of own enumerable properties. Any nested object or array is shared. `structuredClone` handles most structures (not functions or DOM nodes) and is built into modern runtimes.

cards.prompt: `a?.b` returns undefined instead of throwing when `a` is null or ___.
cards.answer: undefined
cards.explanation: Optional chaining short-circuits on exactly two values: `null` and `undefined`. It pairs with `??` (nullish coalescing), which falls back only on those same two values — unlike `||`, which also fires on `0`, `''` and `false`.

modules.name: The Event Loop & Async
modules.description: Tasks, microtasks, promises and the ordering rules that decide when your code runs.

cards.prompt: What does this print, and why in that order?
cards.explanation: Synchronous code runs first (1, 4). Then the **microtask** queue drains completely — promise callbacks (3). Only then does the event loop take the next **macrotask**, the timer callback (2). Microtasks always beat timers, no matter the delay.

cards.prompt: This takes 10 seconds instead of 1. Why, and how do you fix it?
cards.answer: `await` inside the loop serialises the requests. Start them all first and await together: `await Promise.all(urls.map(u => fetch(u)))`.
cards.explanation: Sequential await is correct when each request depends on the previous one, and wasteful otherwise. Use `Promise.all` for fail-fast parallelism, `Promise.allSettled` when partial failure is acceptable, and a concurrency limiter when the target has rate limits.

cards.prompt: What are the states of a Promise, and which transitions are legal?
cards.answer: Pending → fulfilled (with a value) or rejected (with a reason). Settlement is permanent — a promise can never change state again or settle twice.
cards.explanation: That immutability is what makes promises composable: attaching `.then` after settlement still fires, and the value cannot be retracted. An unhandled rejection is a warning in browsers and, by default, a fatal error in modern Node.

cards.prompt: The try/catch never fires. Why?
cards.answer: `forEach` ignores the returned promises, so the async callbacks run detached — their rejections become unhandled rejections outside the try block. Use `for...of` with `await`, or `await Promise.all(items.map(...))`.
cards.explanation: `try/catch` only catches synchronous throws in its own frame. An async callback returns a promise immediately; the throw happens later, on a different tick, with nobody listening. No array method awaits its callback — `map` merely returns the promises so that you can hand them to `Promise.all`.

cards.prompt: Debounce vs throttle
cards.answer: Debounce waits for silence before firing once; throttle fires at most once per interval during activity.

left.title: Debounce
points: Resets a timer on every event
Can starve forever under constant input

right.title: Throttle
points: Fires at a fixed maximum rate

cards.explanation: Ask what the user should see: nothing until they pause (debounce) or steady updates while they act (throttle). Getting this backwards is a common source of janky or unresponsive UI.

modules.name: Modern JavaScript & Runtime
modules.description: Modules, iteration protocols, memory and the runtime facts behind everyday code.

cards.prompt: ES Modules vs CommonJS
cards.answer: ESM is static, asynchronous and live-bound; CommonJS is dynamic, synchronous and value-copied.

left.title: ESM (import/export)
points: Live bindings: importer sees later mutations

right.title: CJS (require/module.exports)
points: Resolved at runtime, can be conditional
Copies the value at require time

cards.explanation: The static structure is the whole point: bundlers can only tree-shake and split what they can see without running your code. Mixing them (`require` of ESM) is where most Node packaging pain comes from.

cards.prompt: What makes an object usable with `for...of` and spread?
cards.answer: A `[Symbol.iterator]()` method returning an iterator — an object with `next()` that yields `{ value, done }`. Generator functions produce one for free.
cards.explanation: `for...of`, spread, destructuring, `Array.from`, `Promise.all` and `yield*` all speak this protocol. Implementing it makes a custom collection behave like a built-in. `for...in`, by contrast, walks enumerable string keys including inherited ones — rarely what you want.

cards.prompt: `Map` vs plain object as a dictionary
cards.answer: Map takes any key type, preserves insertion order, has `size`, and has no prototype keys to collide with.

left.title: Map
points: Keys of any type, including objects

cards.explanation: Use a Map for a real keyed collection that grows at runtime, an object for a struct with known fields. `Object.create(null)` removes the prototype hazard if you must use an object as a dictionary.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.explanation: Every JS number is an IEEE-754 double. 0.1 and 0.2 are not exactly representable in binary, so their sum is not exactly 0.3. Past 2^53 the gap between representable integers is 2, so `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2` rounds back to 9007199254740992 — the same value as `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1`. Use `BigInt` for exact large integers and integer cents for money.

cards.prompt: A single-page app grows to 2 GB after an hour of navigation. What are the usual suspects?
cards.answer: Listeners and timers never removed, detached DOM nodes still referenced by JS, unbounded caches/arrays, and closures capturing large objects.
cards.explanation: GC frees only unreachable objects. An `addEventListener` on `window`, a `setInterval`, or a module-level array holds references forever. Fix by removing listeners on teardown (AbortController signals make this one line), clearing timers, and bounding caches — `WeakMap`/`WeakRef` where the key's lifetime should drive the entry's.

modules.name: Values, Types & Functions
modules.description: Primitives, coercion, scoping, functions and the quirks every JavaScript developer meets.

cards.prompt: What are JavaScript's primitive types, and what is everything else?
cards.answer: Seven primitives: `string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`, `undefined`, `null` and `symbol`. Everything else — arrays, functions, dates, maps — is an object, passed and compared by reference.
cards.explanation: Primitives are immutable and compared by value; objects are compared by identity, so `{} === {}` is false. Primitives temporarily wrap in objects when you call methods on them (`"abc".toUpperCase()`), which is why they appear to have methods.

resources.title: MDN — JavaScript data types and data structures

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.answer:
object
function
number
object
true
cards.explanation: `typeof null === "object"` is a bug from the first JavaScript implementation that can never be fixed without breaking the web. `NaN` is a number. Arrays report `"object"`, so test with `Array.isArray`. Test for null with `x === null`, and for "null or undefined" with `x == null`.

cards.prompt: `var` vs `let` vs `const`
cards.answer: `var` is function-scoped and hoisted as `undefined`; `let` and `const` are block-scoped and in the temporal dead zone until declared. `const` forbids reassignment, not mutation.

left.title: var
points: Function scope — leaks out of blocks
Creates a property on the global object at top level

right.title: let / const
points: Temporal dead zone before the declaration

cards.explanation: Default to `const`, use `let` when you genuinely reassign, and never `var` in new code. `const arr = []; arr.push(1)` is legal — freeze with `Object.freeze` (shallowly) if you need immutability.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.answer:
0
fallback
0
[]
true
cards.explanation: The falsy values are `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN` — everything else, including `[]`, `{}` and `"0"`, is truthy. `||` falls back on any falsy value, which silently replaces a legitimate `0`; `??` falls back only on null or undefined.

cards.prompt: Arrow functions vs `function` declarations
cards.answer: Arrows have lexical `this`, `arguments` and `super`, cannot be constructed with `new`, and have no `prototype`. Regular functions get `this` from the call site and are hoisted when declared.

right.title: `function` / method
points: `this` decided by how it is called

cards.explanation: Use arrows for callbacks and small expressions — especially inside methods, where you want the enclosing `this`. Use regular functions (or class methods) for object methods that need their own receiver, constructors, and generators.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.answer:
3 8080 localhost
1 [ 2, 3 ]
cards.explanation: Destructuring defaults apply only when the value is `undefined` — not for `null`, `0` or `""`. The trailing `= {}` makes the whole options object optional; without it, calling `connect()` throws when destructuring `undefined`. Rest elements collect the remainder into a new array.

cards.prompt: What is a closure, and what is it used for?
cards.answer: A function together with the variables of the scope it was created in. The inner function keeps those variables alive and can read and update them after the outer function has returned.
cards.explanation: Closures give private state without classes (counters, memoisation caches, once-only functions), power callbacks and event handlers, and underlie module patterns and React hooks. The cost: anything a long-lived closure captures stays in memory as long as the closure does.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.explanation: Without a comparator, `Array.prototype.sort` converts elements to strings and compares UTF-16 code units, so `"10" < "2"`. Always pass `(a, b) => a - b` for numbers and `localeCompare` (or `Intl.Collator`) for human text. `sort` mutates in place; `toSorted()` returns a new array.

cards.prompt: What do `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `find`, `some` and `every` return?
cards.answer: `map` a new array of transformed items; `filter` a new array of items passing the test; `reduce` a single accumulated value; `find` the first match or `undefined`; `some`/`every` a boolean, short-circuiting.
cards.explanation: None of them mutate the source array. Always give `reduce` an initial value — without one it throws on an empty array and uses the first element as the accumulator. The mutating methods to watch for are `push`, `splice`, `sort` and `reverse`; ES2023 added non-mutating `toSorted`, `toReversed` and `with`.

cards.prompt: How should you throw and wrap errors in modern JavaScript?
cards.answer: Throw `Error` instances (or subclasses), never strings, so you get a stack trace. When translating a low-level failure, pass the original as `cause`: `throw new Error("config load failed", { cause: err })`.
cards.explanation: Subclass `Error` with a `name` for errors callers branch on. In `catch (e)`, `e` is `unknown` in TypeScript because anything can be thrown — check `e instanceof Error` before reading `.message`. Unhandled promise rejections crash modern Node, so every promise chain needs an owner.

modules.name: Objects, Classes & Iteration
modules.description: Classes, property semantics, generators, promise combinators and the built-in collections.

cards.prompt: What do `#private` fields give you that an underscore convention does not?
cards.answer: Hard privacy enforced by the language: `#balance` cannot be read or written from outside the class body — not even via bracket access or reflection — and accessing it on the wrong object throws a TypeError.
cards.explanation: Classes are syntax over prototypes, but `#` fields are genuinely new semantics. Use `static` for class-level members and static blocks for complex static initialisation. `#x in obj` checks brand membership without throwing.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.explanation: `Object.freeze` is shallow: top-level properties become read-only (assignments throw in strict mode, silently fail otherwise), but nested objects stay mutable. For deep immutability, freeze recursively or use immutable data patterns. ES modules are always strict, which is why the assignment here is wrapped in try/catch.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.explanation: `JSON.stringify` drops properties whose value is `undefined`, a function or a symbol; turns `NaN` and `Infinity` into `null`; calls `toJSON` (so dates become ISO strings); and throws on `BigInt` and on cycles. Round-tripping through JSON is lossy — dates come back as strings — which is why `structuredClone` exists.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.explanation: A generator function (`function*`) returns an iterator that runs lazily, pausing at each `yield`. This one is infinite, which is safe because `take` pulls only five values. Generators make lazy pipelines and custom iterables trivial, and `yield*` delegates to another iterable.

cards.prompt: `Promise.all` vs `allSettled` vs `race` vs `any`
cards.answer: `all` resolves with every value or rejects on the first rejection; `allSettled` always resolves with each outcome; `race` settles with whichever settles first; `any` resolves with the first fulfilment and rejects only if all reject.

left.title: all / allSettled
points: `all`: one rejection loses the other results
`allSettled`: right when partial failure is fine

right.title: race / any
points: `race`: first to settle wins, even a rejection

cards.explanation: None of them cancel the losing promises — the other requests keep running. Pair `race` with an `AbortController` (or use `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` with fetch) so a timeout actually stops the work.

cards.prompt: You need to attach metadata to DOM nodes or objects you do not own without leaking them after they are removed. What do you use?
cards.answer: A `WeakMap` keyed by the object. Entries do not keep keys alive, so when the node or object becomes otherwise unreachable, its metadata is garbage-collected with it.
cards.explanation: WeakMaps are not iterable and have no `size`, because their contents depend on GC timing. A normal `Map` keyed by DOM nodes is a classic leak: removed elements stay reachable through the map forever. `WeakRef` and `FinalizationRegistry` exist for rarer cases.

cards.prompt: What is a `Symbol`, and what are well-known symbols for?
cards.answer: A unique, non-string property key: two symbols with the same description are still different. Well-known symbols such as `Symbol.iterator`, `Symbol.asyncIterator` and `Symbol.toPrimitive` let your objects plug into language protocols.
cards.explanation: Symbol-keyed properties do not collide with string keys and are skipped by `for...in`, `Object.keys` and `JSON.stringify`, which makes them good for library metadata. `Symbol.for(key)` returns a shared symbol from a global registry when you need the same symbol across modules.

cards.prompt: To represent integers beyond 2^53 exactly in JavaScript, use the ___ type, written with an `n` suffix such as `9007199254740993n`.
cards.answer: BigInt
cards.explanation: BigInts have arbitrary precision but cannot be mixed with Numbers in arithmetic (`1n + 1` throws a TypeError), are not supported by `Math`, and cannot be serialised by `JSON.stringify` without a custom replacer. Use them for 64-bit IDs and exact integer maths, not for money with decimals.

modules.name: Browser & Node Runtime
modules.description: The DOM event model, fetch and cancellation, the event loop in Node, and packaging.

cards.prompt: A list has 5,000 rows, each with a delete button, and rows are added dynamically. How do you handle clicks?
cards.answer: Event delegation: attach one listener to the list container and use `event.target.closest("button[data-id]")` to find which row was clicked. It works for rows added later and uses one listener instead of 5,000.
cards.explanation: It relies on bubbling: events fire on the target, then propagate up through its ancestors (after an initial capture phase down from the window). `stopPropagation` breaks delegation for everyone above you, so use it sparingly. Non-bubbling events such as `focus` have bubbling equivalents (`focusin`).

cards.prompt: Why does this treat a 500 response as success?
cards.answer: `fetch` only rejects on network failure — any HTTP status, including 404 and 500, resolves normally. Check `if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`)` before parsing, and add a timeout with `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000)`.
cards.explanation: The other classic fetch traps: calling `res.json()` on an error page that returns HTML, forgetting that the body can be read only once, and omitting `credentials` when cookies are needed cross-origin. Without an abort signal, a hung request waits indefinitely.

cards.prompt: What is `AbortController` for?
cards.answer: Cancellation: `controller.signal` is passed to fetch, event listeners, streams and your own async functions; `controller.abort()` cancels them all, rejecting pending work with an `AbortError`.
cards.explanation: Typical uses: cancel the previous search request when the user types again, abort in-flight requests when a component unmounts, and remove many listeners at once with `addEventListener(type, fn, { signal })`. `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` and `AbortSignal.any([...])` cover timeouts and combined signals.

cards.prompt: Run as a CommonJS script (`node app.cjs`), what does this print?
cards.answer:
sync
nextTick
promise
timeout
cards.explanation: Node drains the `process.nextTick` queue before the promise microtask queue, and both before moving on to the next event-loop phase (timers, I/O poll, `setImmediate` check). Twist: as an ES module the order becomes sync, promise, nextTick, because module evaluation itself runs inside a microtask. Recursive `nextTick` calls can starve I/O entirely — prefer `queueMicrotask` or `setImmediate` in library code.

cards.prompt: A Node service reads a 4 GB log file with `fs.readFile` and crashes. What should it do instead?
cards.answer: Stream it: `fs.createReadStream` plus `readline`, or `stream.pipeline` through transforms, processes the file in chunks with constant memory. `readFile` loads the entire file into one buffer.
cards.explanation: Streams also provide backpressure — a fast producer pauses when a slow consumer's buffer fills. Use `pipeline` (or `for await` over a readable) rather than bare `.pipe()`, which does not forward errors or clean up on failure.

cards.prompt: A Node API endpoint resizes images in pure JavaScript, and every other request stalls while it runs. What is wrong, and what fixes it?
cards.answer: CPU-bound work blocks the single event-loop thread, so nothing else is served until it finishes. Move it off the loop: a `worker_threads` pool, a separate process or queue worker, or a native library that works on the libuv thread pool.
cards.explanation: Node is fast for I/O because one thread multiplexes many waiting sockets, and that same design makes it poor at long computations on the main thread. Measure event-loop lag (`perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay`) to detect it in production.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between `dependencies`, `devDependencies` and `peerDependencies`?
cards.answer: `dependencies` are needed at runtime; `devDependencies` only for building and testing (not installed for consumers of a library); `peerDependencies` must be provided by the host project — plugins declare the framework they plug into this way, so only one copy is installed.
cards.explanation: For applications the split mainly controls production install size (`npm ci --omit=dev`). `"type": "module"` makes `.js` files ESM, and `"exports"` defines a package's public entry points, hiding internal files.

cards.prompt: What does strict mode change, and when is it on automatically?
cards.answer: It turns silent failures into errors (assigning to read-only or undeclared variables throws), makes `this` undefined in plain function calls instead of the global object, forbids `with` and duplicate parameter names, and reserves future keywords.
cards.explanation: ES modules and class bodies are always strict, so most modern code already runs strict without writing `"use strict"`. The biggest practical effect is that a typo in a variable name throws a ReferenceError instead of creating an accidental global.

cards.prompt: This greeting works in testing. What is the bug, and what should it use instead?
cards.answer: `innerHTML` parses the string as HTML, so a name like `` runs attacker script — DOM-based XSS. Use `textContent` (or build elements with `createElement`) for untrusted text; reserve `innerHTML` for trusted, sanitised markup.
cards.explanation: The core DOM toolkit: `querySelector`/`querySelectorAll` to find elements, `textContent` to set text, `classList` and `setAttribute` for attributes, `createElement` + `append` to build nodes, and `addEventListener` for events. Batch DOM writes and avoid reading layout in between to prevent layout thrashing.
